abstract:
Researchers developed innovative medical gloves with microscopic fluid-repelling surfaces that reduce bacterial attachment and transmission by up to 99%, potentially helping prevent hospital-acquired infections.

The post Engineered Medical Gloves Cut Bacterial Transmission by Up to 99% appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Julianna LeMieux, PhD

content.value:
Microbial infections present a constant threat in the clinic, particularly given the rise of antimicrobial resistance. Health workers follow stringent sanitary guidelines to minimize the spread of bacteria, but infections still spread from one patient to another. Microbes commonly transmit via surfaces such as the hands of health workers, even though they use medical gloves and proper gloving protocols. Although there are some gloves with antimicrobial properties, these gloves don’t eliminate transmission and often lose their antimicrobial properties after a short amount of time.

Now, researchers have manufactured fluid-repelling medical gloves with a unique surface that curbs the transmission of bacteria by as much as 99%. With further work, the gloves could combat the surface spread of pathogens from healthcare workers in hospitals and other healthcare settings.

This work is published in Science Translational Medicine in the paper, “Reduced microbial touch transmission by engineering the microtopography of medical glove surfaces.”

The researchers engineered commercial medical gloves with microscopic surface features—superhydrophobic (Cassie-­ Baxter) microtopographies—that prevent microbes from attaching themselves. Unlike the smooth surfaces of normal gloves, the new gloves feature arrays of tiny posts and grooves that repel droplets of fluids, biofilms, and other microbe-transmitting mediums. They then tested the gloves for rates of microbial attachment and transmission.

More specifically, “Molded post and groove topographies with critical dimensions between 2.5 and 15 micrometers were evaluated through compressive touch experiments with six clinically relevant microbial species (Candida albicans, Enterococcus faecium, Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Staphylococcus epidermidis).

The gloves curtailed the transfer of all six species of bacteria that cause healthcare-associated infections by 97.8%. Furthermore, the gloves also reduced repeated touch transmission over multiple surfaces by as much as 99% for the bacteria Staphylococcus aureus and Klebsiella pneumoniae. In addition, touch transmission from dry biofilms and hospital bedrail surfaces was similarly reduced.

These reductions in microbial attachment and transfer, the authors note, show promise in these modified gloves contributing to reducing pathogen transmission within hospitals.

“The main strategy currently implemented to reduce microbial transmission through touch contact is increased awareness and guidance,” they write. “Our technology helps to mitigate this variability without the need for changes in human behavior.”
